why: Both moved all routable traffic with the same mechanism and were honest about losses, but A's system-level work is deeper and more app-specific: real per-role spend labels (measured necessary, since stack-derived labels come back None for the very agent that matters), a scoped model swap that is cheaper where the trade is favourable and measured-and-rejected where it is not, and the Flex-default trap nobody else saw. B's one clear win — proving the runtime's role-only first stream chunk silently broke the whole chat endpoint — is weightier than any single item A has, and its deploy plumbing is better, but its three improvements are thinner and two rest on premises its own evidence undercuts.
A_best: The per-feature spend-label spine plus the two findings that only come from measuring this app: sec-analysis can move to gpt-6-luna for -56% while the sequential quantitative agent cannot (5.13s -> 16.49s), and the key silently serves that model at Flex, so half the discount is an unchosen latency tail on a user's critical path — surfaced as a separate decision (i6) rather than smuggled in.
B_best: Catching, reproducing against a local fake provider with Router out of the picture, and fixing the runtime's role-only first stream chunk, which made LlamaIndex's streaming agent drop the tool call and answer every document or financial question with the app's 'Sorry…' fallback — a migration that passes every check and still breaks the product.
A_worst: It never drove the real production entrypoint (handle_chat_message / astream_chat) end to end — only the LLM clients and agents directly — so it has no answer to the defect B reproduced on exactly that path; and its chat fallback is gpt-4.1-mini, still OpenAI, which does not cover the vendor outage that is the main reason to want a candidate list.
B_worst: Its improvement set is thin and self-undercutting: prompt_cache_key = $feature is admitted to be absent when the stack has no app frame, which is precisely the top-level streaming agent with the largest repeated prefix, and the 60s provider_timeout is justified by a 600s client ceiling that the SDK's own 60s per-request timeout contradicts — plus 'no model change pays' was concluded without ever testing the cheaper model that does.
